extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, students of poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic drama: definition, constituent elements, and formal requirements (plot unity, character, diction, song, spectacle, magnitude, metre). Intended to guide creation and evaluation of tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy (representation of an action)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tragedy is, then, a representation of an action that is heroic and complete and of a certain magnitude — by means of language enriched with all kinds of ornament... it represents men in action and does not use narrative, and through pity and fear it effects relief to these and similar emotions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that tragedy is principally the representation of an action (not merely character-study or narrative). Language should be enriched (rhythm, tune/song, diction). The emotional aim is to produce pity and fear (catharsis). Tragedy must be enacted by living agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (arrangement of incidents) — primary element
rubrics_metrics.description: "By 'plot' I mean here the arrangement of the incidents... The most important of these is the arrangement of the incidents, for tragedy is not a representation of men but of a piece of action... the incidents and the plot are the end at which tragedy aims... the plot then is the first principle and as it were the soul of tragedy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must be unified, coherent, and focused on a single action; it is the principal determiner of a tragedy's quality. Reversals and discoveries are parts of plot. Writers often achieve diction/character before plot; arranging incidents is harder and essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and organicity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: "A representation of a piece of action must represent a single piece of action and the whole of it; and the component incidents must be so arranged that if one of them be altered or removed, the unity of the whole is disturbed and destroyed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is not ensured merely by having a single hero; incidents must be necessarily or probably connected. Avoid extraneous episodes (those that do not lead to or follow from others). Every incident should make a visible difference to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning, middle and end (wholeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A whole is what has a beginning and middle and end. A beginning is that which is not a necessary consequent of anything else... An end on the contrary is that which is inevitably or, as a rule, the natural result of something else... a middle follows something else and something follows from it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots so that events follow in a natural or probable sequence: beginnings should set up subsequent events, middles should lead to ends, and ends should be natural results. Avoid arbitrary starts or finishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (proper size and graspability)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A thing may be a whole and yet have no magnitude... beauty consists in magnitude and arrangement... The magnitude which admits of a change from bad fortune to good or from good fortune to bad... that is the proper limit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should be large enough to allow significant change (reversal of fortune) but small enough to be grasped at once by memory/audience. Length for performance/competition is a separate practical concern; the 'natural' limit is governed by dramatic magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (secondary but necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Character' is that which determines the quality of the agents... Character is that which reveals choice, shows what sort of thing a man chooses or avoids in circumstances where the choice is not obvious."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be consistent and revealed through choices in non-obvious situations; good speeches alone do not convey character if they show no choice. Character serves the action and is subordinate to plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — reasoned content of speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Thought' appears wherever in the dialogue they put forward an argument or deliver an opinion... 'Thought' means the ability to say what is possible and appropriate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is realized in speeches that present arguments, opinions, or reasoning appropriate to the circumstances. It is analogous to the statesman's or rhetorician's function and contributes to the play's persuasiveness and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (language, verbal expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: "By 'diction' I mean here the metrical arrangement of the words; by 'language' I mean the expression of meaning in words, and this is essentially the same in verse and in prose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction concerns word choice, phrasing, and metrical arrangement. It must express meaning clearly and suitably; excellence in diction is valuable but subordinate to the arrangement of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song-making (melody/musical element)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of the other elements which 'enrich' tragedy the most important is song-making... by 'song-making' I use [the term] in the full, obvious sense of the word."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music/song is integral to tragic effect and produces effects distinct from diction. Some parts of the play's emotional impact are achieved through song; treat song as a major enriching element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (visual/manner of representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Since the representation is performed by living persons, one essential part of a tragedy is the spectacular effect... scenic display, while highly effective, is yet quite foreign to the art and has nothing to do with poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle (staging, scenery, masks, costumes) contributes to effect but is the least poetic element; its craft is closer to the stage-carpenter than to the poet. Do not rely on spectacle to compensate for weak plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals and discoveries (mechanisms of emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two of the most important elements in the emotional effect of tragedy, 'reversals' and 'discoveries,' are parts of the plot."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-constructed reversals (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis) within the plot to produce effective pity and fear. These are chief tools for achieving catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation not narrative (mode of delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It represents men in action and does not use narrative... the representation is performed by living persons..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should dramatize events rather than rely on narrated summary; the action should be shown through performed scenes and speech, emphasising immediacy and enactment rather than telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions and appropriate subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "The latter [comedy] sets out to represent people as worse than they are to-day, the former as better... Comedy is a representation of inferior people... It consists in some blunder or ugliness that does not cause pain or disaster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subject-matter appropriate to the genre: tragedy treats heroic/better-than-average actions and incur suffering suited to pity/fear; comedy treats the laughable/ugly that causes no true harm. Meter, tone, and treatment should align with the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre and stylistic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on metre: iambic is conversational and fits dialogue; hexameter is suited to epic (narrative); trochaic tetrameter suited to satyr plays and dance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre to fit function: conversational scenes favor iambic, elevated narrative favors hexameter, choral/dance passages require meters that suit movement. Meter supports the mode (dialogue vs song vs dance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and exclusion (design of incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Selection and design are necessary for any work of 'representation.'... those who wrote whole-lives or compendia erred by including episodes that do not make up a unity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally select incidents that contribute to the unified action; omit episodes that do not contribute to the causal/probable sequence. Good selection is part of constructing a successful plot.
